title: The Pond That Sleeps
text:
The Scarlet Lotus Pavilion does not boast of its anaesthetic arts. Outsiders would say 'of course — they are demonic; they do not care who is in pain.' That is not the reason.

The reason is the Sleeping-Water pill, which the Pavilion's apothecaries have brewed for three hundred years. A drop on the tongue and the drinker goes quiet; two drops, and the drinker sleeps; three, and the drinker's breath is a thing the room forgets. The formula demands silt from a still lake whose surface stirs *in advance* of a visitor — the Pale Lake is one such; their own pond is another. A lake that remembers who is coming, the old texts say, is a lake that has already learned to listen.

Who is given the pill? The sutra will not say. The apothecaries will not say. What is said, by Red Feather once, at a late cup: 'We give it to those for whom the alternative would be a scream that would travel further than the Pavilion could afford to let it travel.'

She did not clarify whether the carrier of the scream was a captive, a disciple, or a petitioner.

She did not need to.

title: The Red That Does Not Clot
text:
From the old apothecaries' margin-note, copied twice before its ink ran out:

*'In every creek of blood-lotus, one bud will not open. It is not dying. It is not poisoned. It has, of its own small volition, refused. The petals are sealed around a weight the creek did not give them — a weight from somewhere else.

We call the bud_red-that-does-not-clot_ because ground into a draught it will hold shut a wound the heart has already given up on. The body does not know it is being treated. The body knows only that the bleeding has been outvoted.

There is a cost. The bud is the creek's refusal made visible. When you pick it, the creek will not refuse again for a season. What was held back — rain, or grief, or a lifelong patience — is let go.

Pick only one. Pick only when the patient is the reason. And do not, do not, drink it yourself to test its bitterness. The pond does not give back what you would find there.'*

Weilan's note, in the margin: *I have picked one. My hands still smell of it. I did not drink.*

title: The Pestle Unbroken
text:
Weiyan of the Azure Cloud was Weilan's elder sister by four years and by an entire life. She took the cranes when she was fourteen; he took the cinnabar when he was eighteen; between those two moments they did not see one another, and they did not write, and they did not speak of each other to anyone who could have carried a word.

At the last Crane-Lotus clash — fourteen years ago now, when the cranes came down to the creek and the pond came up to the bridge — Weiyan was the physician the Azure Cloud had sent to tend the wounded on the south side. She died between the second and third bells, not in the fighting but at her stretchers; a stray bolt found the tent. Baixu's disciples carried her home.

The pestle on Weilan's shelf is her travelling pestle. It was returned to him by an Azure Cloud courier with no message — only the mortar, wrapped in a physician's silk, placed on the pavilion steps an hour before dawn.

He has never washed it. The last thing she ground is still in the bowl. He has not yet decided whether he wants to know what it was.

title: The Sister's Unspoken Cure
text:
Elder Baixu holds the pestle under the light of the west window for a long time. He smells the residue without touching it. He closes his eyes.

'She was working on a cure,' he says finally, 'for the boiling — for those who had taken too much of the Pavilion's Heart-Boiling Technique and could not sit down afterwards. The formula is not one the Azure Cloud had. It is not one the Pavilion had either; they do not cure what they sell. The residue is a corrective. It would have unmade a weapon your sect did not know it needed unmade.'

He hands the mortar back.

'She did not betray the cranes by making it. She did not betray the pond. She betrayed, perhaps, the idea that there is anything between the two that a good physician cannot cross. Tell her brother — I remember her hand. The knot at the end of the mortar's cord was hers; she tied her bandages the same way. Tell him the residue is a cure, and that I am glad he did not wash it.'

He does not say: *tell him her work was not finished*. He does not need to. Weilan will know the moment he sees the mortar returned.
